title: OO design and Clean ABAP
intro: Explain object orientation through responsibilities, replaceable dependencies, and observable behavior. Memorized definitions become useful when you can name a concrete tradeoff. The examples are hypothetical design exercises, not claims about personal project experience; project naming conventions are separate from the SAP language.

questions.question: Explain abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism with one example.
questions.answer: For a delivery service, abstraction exposes a send operation while hiding transport details. Encapsulation protects its internal state and invariants. Inheritance can specialize a genuine base contract. Polymorphism lets the caller invoke send through an interface while different implementations deliver by different channels. These ideas help changes stay local to the responsible component.
questions.detail: A notification coordinator can receive an email sender or a test sender through the same interface. The coordinator should not inspect the concrete class to decide how to send; doing that would weaken the polymorphic design.
questions.pitfall: Encapsulation means protecting valid behavior and state, not merely generating getters and setters for every attribute.

questions.question: What can an ABAP interface contain, and when would you use one?
questions.answer: An ABAP interface defines a contract implemented by classes. It can declare methods and other components such as types, constants, attributes, and events; it is not limited to abstract methods. I normally keep behavioral interfaces narrow so callers depend on the capability they need and tests can supply a substitute implementation.
questions.detail: A price-provider interface can expose a calculation operation without publishing database access. Two implementations need not be similar classes overall; sharing the required business contract is enough. Ordinary interfaces and specialized BAdI interfaces have different restrictions.
questions.pitfall: An interface is not an abstract class, and a collection of similarly named methods alone does not establish a meaningful common contract.

questions.question: How do ABSTRACT and FINAL affect classes and methods?
questions.answer: An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly and may provide shared implementation. It does not have to contain an abstract method. An abstract method has no implementation there and must be implemented before a concrete subclass can be instantiated. FINAL prevents further subclassing for a class, or further redefinition for a method.
questions.detail: An abstract document processor could implement logging while requiring a concrete processing step. If no supported specialization is intended, a final class communicates that choice. Marking a class final does not stop it implementing interfaces or receiving collaborators.
questions.pitfall: Do not import another language's virtual keyword or method-overloading rules into ABAP; use ABAP's actual redefinition and signature rules.

questions.question: How do upcasting and downcasting work in ABAP Objects?
questions.answer: Upcasting views an object through a compatible superclass or interface reference and preserves the same object. Downcasting requests a more specific compatible type and can fail at runtime if the actual object does not support it. I use a type check or handle CX_SY_MOVE_CAST_ERROR when a downcast is genuinely necessary.
questions.detail: A reference typed to a payment interface can point to a card implementation. Converting it back to the card type does not create a new card object. Frequent downcasts often indicate the interface is missing a required capability or the caller knows too much.
questions.pitfall: Casting a reference changes the accessible static view, not the object's dynamic type or stored data.

questions.question: What is the difference between instance and static methods and constructors?
questions.answer: An instance method acts on an object and can access its instance state. A static method belongs to the class and has no implicit current instance. The instance constructor initializes a newly created object. The class constructor initializes class-level state when the runtime first requires it in the internal session; I avoid unpredictable heavy work there.
questions.detail: A class can contain static and instance methods together. Restricting creation or declaring a class abstract affects instantiation; merely adding CLASS-METHODS does not. Constructor injection makes mandatory dependencies visible before business methods are called.
questions.pitfall: ABAP does not make a class uninstantiable simply because it has static methods, and class data is not automatically shared system-wide.

questions.question: When do you prefer composition over inheritance?
questions.answer: I prefer composition when behavior varies independently or I want to replace a dependency without coupling classes to a hierarchy. Inheritance is appropriate when the subclass really preserves the base contract and specialization is intentional. Composition makes ownership and collaboration explicit and avoids a deep hierarchy used only to share a few helper methods.
questions.detail: A report service can contain a repository, an authorization policy, and a formatter. Different implementations can be supplied independently. Making every report inherit from a large superclass may entangle unrelated persistence, output, and authorization decisions.
questions.pitfall: Code reuse alone is weak justification for inheritance; a subclass that violates caller expectations is not a sound substitute.

questions.question: How do dependency injection and dependency inversion differ?
questions.answer: Dependency inversion is a design principle: business policy should depend on suitable abstractions rather than concrete infrastructure details. Dependency injection is a way to supply a collaborator from outside, commonly through a constructor. Together they make dependencies visible and replaceable, but injection alone does not guarantee a useful abstraction or a good responsibility split.
questions.detail: An approval service receives a repository interface. Production composition supplies a database implementation; an ABAP Unit test supplies a controlled double. The service should not immediately instantiate its own concrete repository and ignore the injected dependency.
questions.pitfall: Injecting a concrete class everywhere may aid construction while still leaving the business layer tightly coupled to infrastructure.

questions.question: How would you apply SOLID without overengineering?
questions.answer: I use SOLID as questions about change. Does each component have a coherent responsibility? Can variation be added without repeatedly editing central logic? Do substitutes preserve expectations? Are interfaces small enough for their clients? Do business rules depend on abstractions? I introduce structure to solve an observed need, not to maximize the number of classes.
questions.detail: Separating tax calculation from database retrieval can support focused tests and independent changes. Creating an interface for a tiny stable helper with no substitution need may add little value. Discuss one concrete change scenario rather than reciting five slogans.
questions.pitfall: Single responsibility does not mean one method per class, and open/closed does not mean existing code must never be changed.

questions.question: When are Strategy and Factory useful?
questions.answer: Strategy packages interchangeable behavior behind a common contract, such as choosing a pricing rule. A factory centralizes construction when callers should not know concrete classes or setup details. They often work together: configuration selects a strategy that a factory creates. A simple static creation helper is not automatically the inheritance-based Factory Method pattern.
questions.detail: For domestic and export pricing, the coordinator receives a pricing strategy. The composition boundary decides which implementation is appropriate. If only one simple construction path exists, direct construction outside the business logic may be clearer than an elaborate factory hierarchy.
questions.pitfall: Do not call every method that returns an object Factory Method without distinguishing a simple factory from the formal pattern.

questions.question: What do Adapter and Facade solve in SAP integration code?
questions.answer: An adapter translates one contract into another, allowing a client to use an existing service through its preferred interface. A facade offers a simpler operation over a subsystem with several steps. For a legacy posting API, either pattern can isolate mapping and error translation while keeping its transaction, authorization, and release limitations visible.
questions.detail: A posting facade might coordinate validation and mapping; an adapter can translate an application's request into a legacy function module's structures. The caller still needs to know whether persistence is synchronous and who owns commit and rollback.
questions.pitfall: Wrapping an unreleased SAP object does not by itself make that underlying dependency released, cloud compliant, or clean-core Level A.

questions.question: What are the limitations of Singleton in ABAP?
questions.answer: A conventional singleton restricts construction and returns a stored instance through a class-level accessor. Its scope is normally the ABAP internal session, not the whole SAP landscape. It can introduce hidden dependencies, persistent mutable test state, and difficult substitution. I use it only when that lifetime and access model are deliberate requirements.
questions.detail: A configuration cache might need invalidation when customizing changes. A singleton that retains yesterday's assumptions or leaks state between tests becomes a correctness problem. Often an explicitly constructed shared service with an injected interface gives clearer ownership.
questions.pitfall: A singleton does not synchronize business updates across sessions, work processes, application servers, or users.

questions.question: How do ABAP OO events differ from durable business events?
questions.answer: An ABAP OO event notifies registered handlers in the current runtime context and can decouple a publisher from listeners. A durable business event used for workflow or external integration needs a separate delivery mechanism, transaction coordination, monitoring, and retry design. Similar terminology does not mean a local event provides durable asynchronous messaging.
questions.detail: An ALV interaction can raise an event handled by a controller registered with SET HANDLER. Starting an external approval process after a document save requires the supported business-event or integration mechanism, including handling duplicates and failures.
questions.pitfall: RAISE EVENT by itself does not persist a message or guarantee workflow creation after a commit.

questions.question: What would you change first in a difficult legacy ABAP method?
questions.answer: I first identify its observable behavior, callers, and transaction responsibilities. Then I make small, reviewable improvements such as naming unclear concepts, separating a calculation from I/O, and removing repeated logic. I add focused tests around risky behavior before larger restructuring. Preserving the established contract matters more than turning every statement into modern syntax.
questions.detail: A safe extraction might isolate discount calculation while keeping posting and commit behavior unchanged. In this project, new tables use lt_, structures ls_, and constants co_; these are team preferences, not mandatory ABAP syntax or universal Clean ABAP rules.
questions.pitfall: A broad stylistic rewrite without behavior evidence can introduce regressions and make review harder, even if the result looks more modern.

questions.question: How do you make an OO design testable, and what should ABAP Unit assert?
questions.answer: I separate business decisions from database, clock, authorization, and external-service access through appropriate seams. Tests exercise observable behavior with controlled inputs and meaningful assertions. I cover boundaries, failures, and interactions that matter to the contract. Coverage helps identify untested areas, but it does not prove that assertions are correct or that real integration works.
questions.detail: For an approval policy, test below, at, and above a threshold, plus a missing approver. A repository double can simulate not-found and technical failure. Separate integration checks must verify the real persistence and authorization behavior in the target system.
questions.pitfall: A test that only asserts that a method returned, or mirrors its implementation step by step, provides weak evidence.

questions.question: How does MVC separate responsibilities?
questions.answer: The Model represents application data and relevant behavior. The View presents information and collects interaction. The Controller interprets user interaction and coordinates model and view changes. Frameworks implement the pattern differently; MVC is a responsibility split, not a fixed network sequence that every application follows.
questions.detail: In SAPUI5, a controller can handle a button press while a bound model supplies view data. Backend business rules still belong in the appropriate service or BO, not only in the browser controller.
questions.pitfall: MVC does not mean copying all backend business logic into the UI controller or assuming the view must always be manually rebuilt.
